questions.q: A 25-year-old man presents with a painless ulcer on his penis with indurated edges for 2 weeks. Dark-field microscopy of the exudate shows motile spirochetes. Which statement about the causative organism is most accurate?
opts: It can be grown on standard blood agar
It is detected by VDRL which becomes non-reactive after treatment within 3 months
The organism is Treponema pallidum, an obligate human pathogen that cannot be cultured in vitro
Penicillin allergy is a contraindication even in pregnancy
questions.exp: Treponema pallidum causes primary syphilis. It cannot be cultured on artificial media. Dark-field microscopy is the gold standard for primary chancre diagnosis. VDRL may remain reactive for years after treatment.

questions.q: A 35-year-old farmer develops a painless papule on his finger that progresses to a central black eschar with marked surrounding oedema but no pain. He works with cattle hides. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Cutaneous anthrax (Bacillus anthracis) presents as a painless black eschar with marked gelatinous, non-pitting oedema and no lymphangitis. Occupational exposure to animal products is classic. Ecthyma gangrenosum is caused by Pseudomonas and is painful with septicaemia context.

questions.q: A 40-year-old immunocompromised patient develops dermatomal vesicles on the chest with post-herpetic neuralgia. Which antiviral and dosing is correct for treatment of Herpes zoster in an immunocompetent adult?
opts: Valacyclovir 1000 mg three times/day for 7 days
Famciclovir 500 mg once daily for 7 days
questions.exp: Valacyclovir 1000 mg TDS for 7 days is the preferred oral regimen for HZ in immunocompetent adults, offering better bioavailability than acyclovir. Acyclovir for HZ is 800 mg 5 times/day for 7 days (not twice daily).

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman presents with recurrent oral ulcers, genital ulcers, and hypopyon uveitis. The pathergy test is positive. What is the first-line systemic agent for mucocutaneous manifestations?
questions.exp: Colchicine is the first-line treatment for mucocutaneous manifestations of Behcet's disease, particularly for aphthous ulcers and erythema nodosum. Azathioprine is used for ocular and vascular involvement.

questions.q: A 20-year-old student presents with annular scaly plaques on the trunk with central clearing and raised active border. KOH mount shows branching hyphae. What morphological feature distinguishes Trichophyton rubrum from T. mentagrophytes on culture?
opts: T. rubrum produces urease while T. mentagrophytes does not
T. rubrum has granular colony texture and T. mentagrophytes is fluffy
T. rubrum shows a red-pigmented reverse on PDA and negative urease; T. mentagrophytes is urease positive
T. mentagrophytes causes tinea capitis while T. rubrum causes tinea pedis exclusively
questions.exp: T. rubrum produces a characteristic wine-red pigment on the reverse of PDA (potato dextrose agar) and is urease negative. T. mentagrophytes is urease positive. Both can cause tinea corporis.

questions.q: A 45-year-old male with borderline tuberculoid leprosy develops sudden onset of erythematous, tender, slightly raised skin lesions over old hypopigmented patches with acute neuritis. What is this reaction and its first-line treatment?
opts: Type 2 lepra reaction (ENL); treated with thalidomide
Type 1 lepra reaction (reversal reaction); treated with prednisolone
Type 2 lepra reaction; treated with prednisolone
questions.exp: Type 1 (reversal) reaction occurs in borderline leprosy (BT, BB, BL) with sudden upgrading, erythema of existing lesions, and acute neuritis. First-line treatment is prednisolone 40–60 mg/day. ENL (Type 2) occurs in BL/LL and is treated with thalidomide or clofazimine.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman presents with tense bullae on erythematous skin, sparing mucous membranes. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 at the dermoepidermal junction. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid (BP) presents with tense bullae, usually no mucosal involvement, and linear IgG/C3 at the DEJ on DIF. The antigen is BP180 (type XVII collagen) in the lamina lucida. Pemphigus shows intercellular IgG (fish-net pattern).

questions.q: A 30-year-old HIV-positive patient presents with multiple flesh-coloured papules with central umbilication on the face. CD4 count is 80 cells/μL. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Molluscum contagiosum presents with umbilicated papules. In HIV patients with low CD4 counts, lesions are typically large, numerous, and atypical (giant molluscum). The poxvirus (MCV) causes this. Cryptococcosis can mimic MC but scraping and culture differentiates.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man presents with an ulcerated nodule on the lower lip with rolled, everted edges. Biopsy shows nests of atypical squamous cells invading the dermis with keratin pearls. What is the single most important prognostic factor?
opts: Depth of invasion (Breslow thickness equivalent) and perineural invasion
questions.exp: For cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, depth of invasion (>2 mm or beyond subcutis) and perineural invasion are the strongest adverse prognostic features. These are incorporated in AJCC high-risk criteria. Lip SCC has higher metastatic potential than sun-exposed trunk.

questions.q: During a patch test, a patient shows a 2+ reaction to potassium dichromate at day 4. Which occupational group is most likely to have this sensitisation?
questions.exp: Potassium dichromate is the most common allergen in construction workers because cement contains hexavalent chromium. Hairdressers are sensitised to p-phenylenediamine (PPD) and persulfates. Rubber workers react to thiurams and mercaptobenzothiazole.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman with known SLE develops a butterfly rash, oral ulcers, and serositis. Skin biopsy of involved skin shows granular IgG at the DEJ. What is this biopsy finding called and what antibody correlates most strongly with renal lupus?
questions.exp: The lupus band test (LBT) refers to granular immunoglobulin deposition at the DEJ on DIF. Anti-dsDNA antibody titres correlate best with disease activity and renal involvement (lupus nephritis). Anti-Sm is specific for SLE but does not correlate with nephritis activity.

questions.q: A 24-year-old woman develops erythema, blistering, and skin necrosis involving >30% BSA with mucosal involvement 2 weeks after starting a sulfonamide antibiotic. Skin biopsy shows full-thickness epidermal necrosis. What is the diagnosis and the eponymous sign for skin detachment?
questions.exp: TEN involves >30% BSA detachment (SJS <10%, overlap 10–30%). Nikolsky sign (lateral pressure causes skin to slide) is positive. Asboe-Hansen sign (pressure on intact bulla causes lateral extension) is positive in both. Full-thickness epidermal necrosis on biopsy differentiates from SSSS.

questions.q: A 35-year-old man presents with hypopigmented anaesthetic macules on the trunk. Slit-skin smear shows 2+ bacillary index (BI). According to WHO, which MDT regimen should be prescribed?
questions.exp: A BI of 2+ indicates multibacillary (MB) leprosy. WHO MB-MDT consists of rifampicin 600 mg monthly (supervised) + dapsone 100 mg daily + clofazimine 300 mg monthly/50 mg daily for 12 months. PB-MDT is for skin smear-negative (PB) cases for 6 months.

questions.q: A 50-year-old woman presents with Raynaud's phenomenon, puffy hands, skin tightening proximal to MCP joints, and telangiectasias. ANA is positive; anti-Scl-70 is positive. What is the most likely diagnosis and its lung complication?
opts: Limited systemic sclerosis; pulmonary arterial hypertension
Diffuse systemic sclerosis; interstitial lung disease (ILD)
Mixed connective tissue disease; pulmonary embolism
questions.exp: Anti-topoisomerase I (anti-Scl-70) antibody is associated with diffuse systemic sclerosis (dcSSc), which causes ILD as the major pulmonary complication. Anti-centromere antibody is associated with limited SSc (CREST syndrome) and pulmonary arterial hypertension.

questions.q: A wood cutter develops a subcutaneous nodule on his hand that slowly enlarges and new nodules appear along the lymphatic channels of the forearm. What is the most likely diagnosis and causative organism?
questions.exp: Sporotrichosis causes a classic sporotrichoid (lymphocutaneous) pattern of ascending nodules along lymphatics after traumatic inoculation with plant material. Sporothrix schenckii is the thermally dimorphic fungus responsible. Treatment is itraconazole 200 mg/day for 3–6 months.

questions.q: A 20-year-old man presents with well-defined, silvery-scaled plaques on the elbows and knees with a positive Auspitz sign. Histology shows Munro's microabscesses and elongated rete ridges. Which interleukin pathway is primarily targeted by biologics used for psoriasis?
questions.exp: Psoriasis is driven predominantly by the IL-23/Th17/IL-17 axis. Biologics targeting this pathway include anti-IL-17A (secukinumab, ixekizumab), anti-IL-17RA (brodalumab), and anti-IL-23p19 (guselkumab, risankizumab). IL-4/IL-13 is targeted in atopic dermatitis (dupilumab).

questions.q: A 3-year-old child presents with honey-coloured crusted lesions around the nose and mouth. Gram stain of exudate shows gram-positive cocci in chains. Culture grows group A beta-haemolytic streptococcus (GABHS). Which complication is unique to streptococcal (not staphylococcal) impetigo?
questions.exp: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) is a specific complication of nephritogenic strains of GABHS impetigo. SSSS and bullous impetigo are caused by staphylococcal exfoliative toxins. Antibiotic treatment of streptococcal impetigo does not prevent PSGN.

questions.q: A 45-year-old man presents with recurrent genital ulcers, lymphadenopathy progressing to inguinal buboes with the groove sign (divided by Poupart's ligament). PCR confirms Chlamydia trachomatis. Which serovars cause lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV)?
questions.exp: C. trachomatis serovars L1, L2, L3 cause LGV. Serovars A–C cause trachoma (ocular). Serovars D–K cause urogenital infections (cervicitis, urethritis, PID). The groove sign (buboes above and below inguinal ligament creating a groove) is pathognomonic of LGV.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman undergoes excision of a 1.2 mm Breslow thickness melanoma on her back with no ulceration (pT1b). What is the recommended surgical excision margin?
questions.exp: Current guidelines (NCCN/British) recommend 1 cm excision margin for melanomas 1.01–2 mm Breslow thickness. For <1 mm, 1 cm is adequate. For >2 mm, 2 cm margins are recommended. 0.5 cm is used for melanoma in situ.

questions.q: A dermatologist uses a handheld device emitting 308 nm monochromatic UVB light to treat a 10-year-old child with localised vitiligo on the face. What is this device called and what is its main advantage over broadband UVB?
opts: NB-UVB (311 nm) phototherapy; fewer sessions needed
Excimer laser/lamp (308 nm); targeted therapy minimising exposure of normal skin
questions.exp: The 308 nm excimer laser (or lamp) delivers targeted monochromatic UVB directly to lesional skin without irradiating surrounding normal skin, allowing higher fluences with fewer treatments. It is especially useful for localised, stable vitiligo. NB-UVB (311 nm) irradiates the whole body.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman on methotrexate for psoriasis develops megaloblastic anaemia and oral ulcers. What is the mechanism of methotrexate-induced folate deficiency and how is it mitigated?
opts: MTX inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), blocking THF synthesis; mitigated by folic acid supplementation
MTX directly depletes serum folate stores; mitigated by folinic acid (leucovorin) given before each dose
MTX impairs intestinal folate absorption; mitigated by B12 supplementation
MTX induces folate excretion in urine; mitigated by probenecid co-administration
questions.exp: MTX inhibits DHFR, preventing reduction of dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate (THF), thus blocking purine/pyrimidine synthesis. Folic acid 5 mg/week (not folinic acid) supplementation reduces mucosal and haematological side effects without significantly reducing efficacy in psoriasis.

questions.q: A patient with cystic acne is started on isotretinoin. Baseline investigations reveal total cholesterol 190 mg/dL, triglycerides 140 mg/dL, LFT normal, and negative pregnancy test. After 2 months, triglycerides rise to 650 mg/dL. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Continue isotretinoin and add omega-3 fatty acids
Reduce isotretinoin dose and add fenofibrate
Stop isotretinoin immediately as TG >500 mg/dL poses pancreatitis risk
Switch to oral doxycycline and topical retinoid
questions.exp: Isotretinoin can elevate serum triglycerides. TG levels >500 mg/dL (some guidelines say >700 mg/dL) risk acute pancreatitis; isotretinoin should be discontinued. TG 400–500 mg/dL may warrant dose reduction with dietary modification. Regular lipid monitoring every 4–6 weeks is essential.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman develops grouped pruritic vesicles on extensor elbows, knees, and buttocks. DIF shows granular IgA at the dermal papillary tips. Jejunal biopsy shows villous atrophy. What is the treatment of choice?
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis (Duhring's disease) is associated with coeliac disease. DIF shows granular IgA at papillary dermis tips. Treatment: dapsone for rapid itch relief + strict gluten-free diet (GFD), which is the only treatment that addresses the underlying enteropathy and may eventually allow dapsone withdrawal.

questions.q: A 48-year-old woman presents with diffuse hair loss following a febrile illness 3 months ago. Hair pull test shows >6 telogen hairs per 25 pulls. Trichoscopy shows predominance of single-hair follicular units. What is the diagnosis and expected outcome?
opts: Acute telogen effluvium; spontaneous recovery in 3–6 months
Anagen effluvium; regrowth after cause removal
questions.exp: Acute telogen effluvium (TE) follows a trigger 2–4 months prior (febrile illness, postpartum, surgery, crash diet). Increased hair shedding is diffuse; the hair pull test is positive (telogen hairs with club-shaped roots). It resolves spontaneously within 3–6 months once the trigger resolves.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male with long-standing psoriatic arthritis is started on a TNF-alpha inhibitor. Which skin condition can paradoxically be induced by this therapy?
questions.exp: Paradoxical psoriasis (new-onset or worsening plaque or palmoplantar pustular psoriasis) is a well-recognised adverse effect of TNF-alpha inhibitors (adalimumab, infliximab, etanercept). The mechanism involves TNF blockade shifting cytokine balance towards IFN-alpha and IL-17 at certain skin sites.

questions.q: A 68-year-old man presents with a pearly, telangiectatic nodule on the nose with a rolled border. Biopsy shows palisading basaloid cells with peripheral nuclear palisading and clefting artefact. What genetic syndrome is associated with multiple such tumours?
questions.exp: Basal cell carcinoma with peripheral palisading and stromal clefting is classic. Multiple BCCs, jaw keratocysts, calcified falx cerebri, and skeletal anomalies characterise Gorlin-Goltz syndrome (PTCH1 gene mutation). Cowden syndrome (PTEN) features trichilemmomas. Muir-Torre (MLH1/MSH2) features sebaceous neoplasms.

questions.q: A 22-year-old woman presents with bilateral bluish-grey macular pigmentation over the cheekbones, temples, and nose, deeper than freckles, sparing the lips and conjunctiva. What is the diagnosis and its pathological location of melanin?
opts: Hori's naevus (acquired bilateral nevus of Ota-like macules); dermal melanocytes in the superficial dermis
Naevus of Ota; periocular dermal melanocytosis
Erythema dyschromicum perstans; melanin in basal layer with lichenoid infiltrate
questions.exp: Hori's naevus (ABNOM) presents as bilateral, bluish-grey macules on malar areas in Asian women, without scleral or mucosal involvement. Melanin is in dermal melanocytes (superficial dermis). Naevus of Ota is unilateral and involves the periocular area. Treatment: Q-switched Nd:YAG laser.

questions.q: A 30-year-old HIV-positive patient from Southeast Asia develops papulonecrotic lesions on the face, upper trunk, and lymphadenopathy. Blood culture grows a thermally dimorphic fungus that produces red pigment on Sabouraud's agar (Marneffei red). What is the treatment of choice?
opts: Itraconazole 200 mg twice daily for 8 weeks
Amphotericin B for 2 weeks followed by itraconazole 400 mg/day for 10 weeks
Voriconazole 200 mg twice daily for 12 weeks
questions.exp: Talaromyces (Penicillium) marneffei is endemic in Southeast Asia and causes disseminated disease in HIV patients. Treatment: IV amphotericin B 0.6 mg/kg/day for 2 weeks (induction), then oral itraconazole 400 mg/day for 10 weeks (consolidation), followed by secondary prophylaxis with itraconazole 200 mg/day.

questions.q: A 25-year-old with new genital warts (condylomata acuminata) is treated with patient-applied imiquimod 5% cream. What is the mechanism of action of imiquimod?
opts: It directly inhibits HPV DNA polymerase
It is a Toll-like receptor 7/8 agonist that stimulates innate and adaptive immunity via IFN-alpha induction
It alkylates HPV viral DNA causing strand breaks
It inhibits keratinocyte proliferation via retinoid receptor activation
questions.exp: Imiquimod is an immune response modifier acting as a TLR7/8 agonist. It activates plasmacytoid dendritic cells and macrophages to produce IFN-alpha, TNF-alpha, and other cytokines, stimulating cell-mediated immunity to clear HPV-infected cells. It has no direct antiviral activity against HPV.

questions.q: A 70-year-old man on long-term hydroxyurea for polycythaemia vera develops painful, non-healing ulcers on the malleoli. Skin biopsy shows no vasculitis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Hydroxyurea causes a well-known cutaneous side effect of painful leg ulcers on malleoli and perimalleolar skin, particularly in elderly patients. The mechanism is not fully understood but involves impaired DNA repair and endothelial dysfunction. Treatment requires discontinuation of hydroxyurea and switching to alternative myelosuppressive therapy.

questions.q: A 35-year-old pregnant woman (28 weeks) presents with intense pruritus and urticarial papules and plaques in the periumbilical striae, sparing the umbilicus. What is the diagnosis and fetal prognosis?
opts: Pemphigoid gestationis; associated with risk of preterm delivery and small-for-gestational-age infant
Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy (PEP/PUPPP); benign with no fetal risk
Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy; risk of sudden intrauterine fetal death
Atopic eruption of pregnancy; mild fetal atopy risk
questions.exp: Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy (PEP), also called PUPPP, presents in primigravidae in the third trimester with urticarial plaques in abdominal striae sparing the umbilicus. It resolves post-partum with no adverse fetal outcome. Pemphigoid gestationis involves the umbilicus and has fetal risks.
